data.title: Access Badges Can Be Cloned
data.summary: Access credentials used legacy technology that transmits a static identifier with no authentication, so a badge could be read covertly at close range and copied onto a blank card that the access control system accepts as genuine.
data.description:
Low-frequency proximity cards, and early high-frequency cards with their published keys, broadcast a fixed number to any reader that asks. There is no challenge, no cryptography and no way for the system to tell an original from a copy.

Reading requires only brief proximity. A concealed long-range reader in a bag collects credentials in a lift, at a reception desk, or while queueing for coffee, and the owner notices nothing. The number is then written to a blank card, and the clone is indistinguishable in the logs from the genuine badge — which also means the legitimate holder appears responsible for whatever follows.

Credentials are also exposed through photographs: badges worn visibly in social media posts and press images often show the card number or enough of the design to forge a convincing visual copy.
data.recommendation:
* Migrate to credentials using mutual authentication and diversified keys (such as DESFire EV2/EV3 or Seos), and disable legacy formats on readers rather than running both.
* Where migration is phased, pair the badge with a PIN or biometric at sensitive doors.
* Require badges to be removed from view outside the building, and ask staff not to photograph them.
* Alert on impossible journeys and on one credential used at distant readers in quick succession.
* Deactivate credentials promptly on departure, and audit active badges against current staff.
data.short_recommendation: Migrate to cryptographic credentials with mutual authentication.
